headline: Oil supply more structurally disrupted than during Russia-Ukraine — effective energy prices for refined products likely to stay elevated and uneven across economies even if headline crude dips
reasoning: Varathan argues the current oil situation is more complex than the Russia-Ukraine episode because availability at the posted price is now in question. Refined products are trading at a significant premium to crude, and OPEC fragmentation means crude flows are increasingly bilateral and access is skewed to more powerful buyers. Global refining capacity is also no longer homogeneous due to ongoing conflicts. His base case is for oil to remain around $100 on sticker prices with the Middle East crisis unresolved, and for effective energy prices (diesel, jet fuel, gasoline) to stay high and unevenly distributed, feeding global inflationary pressures.
quote: We have a bigger issue with oil today than if we were to compare this to Russia, Ukraine, and the primary part of it being is what you see on the screen is not what you get. So $100 oil back in the Russia-Ukraine crisis left fewer questions about whether you can access it at $100, whereas that has become a more prominent question now. And your refined products are selling for far higher compared to the corresponding crude prices. And the short version of that is the flow of crude remains highly disrupted with a fragmenting OPEC. It also means access to it might be on more bilateral terms. And so people with more power can get it more easily. And refining capacity globally is no longer homogeneous because of all the ongoing conflicts, so on and so forth for impact capacity.

reasoning: Varathan notes that the Australian economy is still absorbing the lagged effects of RBA rate hikes, meaning the slowdown observed so far is not complete. He highlights that the RBA is not hiking in isolation — global yields are rising in tandem, amplifying the domestic tightening impact. Consumer confidence is weak despite a resilient jobs market, and further softness is expected to come through over time.

headline: RBA rate hike impacts still feeding through with a lag; pain amplification likely greater in slower sectors versus AI-related growth areas over the next 6–18 months
reasoning: Varathan argues the full impact of RBA rate hikes has not yet been felt, with a lag effect still to materialise. He notes the growth within the economy is increasingly uneven, with AI-related and faster-growing sectors better able to absorb higher rates than slower ones. This unevenness means incremental rate hikes will come with sharper trade-offs, particularly for the housing market (balance sheet) and the labour market (income flows). He sees compounding impacts over the next 6 to 18 months across both dimensions.
quote: Whatever slowdown we are seeing now it's not done yet. We will see more of that construction coming, particularly against the backdrop of global yields rising in tandem. So it's not like it's just the RBA responding. There are many who are belatedly catching up as well. The even more uneven landscape means two things. One is as the leg impact comes through, the pain amplification may be far greater in some parts rather than others. So the one policy tool is going to start hurting more, and incremental rate hikes are going to come at far sharper trade offs, including to the housing market, which is even slower, even more slower moving than the labor market is.

headline: BOJ hikes inflict greater economic pain than Fed hikes as long-end Japanese borrowing costs surge; yen may continue to weaken despite rate rises, with the BOJ's best relief coming from Fed cuts
reasoning: Varathan notes that markets now see BOJ terminal rates closer to 2%, but within the BOJ there is a view that reaching even 1.75% may be a struggle given uneven household conditions and precautionary saving. Crucially, each BOJ hike has been accompanied by a faster rise in long-term Japanese borrowing costs than in the US, amplifying economic pain. As a result, yen appreciation is not guaranteed from BOJ hikes because the associated economic damage offsets the tightening signal. With fiscal risks still present, the yen could continue to weaken even as rates rise, putting the BOJ in the worst possible position. Varathan concludes the BOJ's best outcome is for the Fed to cut, providing yen relief without further BOJ action.
quote: The biggest impact here is each of the BOJ hike hurts a lot more than the Fed's hikes, insofar that your premium for your longer term borrowing costs in Japan has continued to climb through each and every one of these hikes at a far faster pace. And that means two things. One is the economic trade off for the BOJ is far greater. So the yen doesn't always get to benefit from the BOJ hikes in the sense that there's economic pain associated with those hikes even though it comes with inflation being tackled. And whilst the fiscal outlook is still unclear and there are risks to it, then the yen could continue to weaken despite and into higher rates. Which means the BOJ is doing two things, is inflicting pain on the economy without necessarily stabilizing the yen. So that's the worst position to be in. And their best bet is that the fed turns around and starts cutting.

headline: 5% is the new 4% for US 10-year yields — elevated long-end rates likely to persist driven by fiscal concerns and AI capital crowding out government borrowing
reasoning: Varathan argues that US 10-year yields are unlikely to return to the 4–4.5% range even if oil prices retreat, because the move higher is not solely driven by oil. Fiscal concerns and AI-related capital issuance are absorbing liquidity and pushing up Treasury yields. Even when the Fed eventually pivots back to a cutting cycle, the term premium (the spread between 2-year and 10-year rates) is expected to remain above 100 basis points, keeping long-end yields structurally elevated.
quote: If we look back to earlier this year, even when the crisis started in the Middle East, we were looking at, you know, ten year yields being mostly bound within 4 to 4.5%. I don't think we're going to get back there even if oil prices track back to where they were maybe in March, April. So it seems it's difficult to get there. And that's primarily because this is not driven, uh, you know, exclusively by oil. There's also additional worries about, uh, you know, the fiscal stance, uh, there's AI issuance that's mopping up more and more of the available capital and liquidity driving up, uh, you know, the yields in the US Treasury and broader government space. So in a sense, AI crowding out, uh, government borrowing.

headline: Gold struggles near-term as rising real yields and AI return-chasing reduce its appeal, but structural debasement risk keeps long-term bull case intact
reasoning: Varathan notes that the rise in US yields is being driven predominantly by real yields rather than inflation expectations, which is particularly negative for zero-yielding gold. The AI-driven hunt for transformational returns further reduces the relative attractiveness of holding gold. However, he sees a structural bull case for gold that is merely being crowded out: if central banks or public entities ultimately pump liquidity back into the system, debasement risks will return and restore gold's allure. In the near term, gold faces persistent headwinds from elevated real rates.
quote: A zero yielding asset like gold may lose its shine in the near term. And that's what we've seen. Part of that coming through. And the other part of the AI story, I mean, if people are going to chase AI as a transformational technology and say, look, I'm looking for huge returns and so on and so forth. Then holding on to gold at zero yielding becomes less compelling as well. Until and unless you come to a point where you think we go from a place where AI is sucking out all the liquidity to a place where you think central banks or other, uh, you know, public entities are going to pump a lot more liquidity in the system, creating debasement risks and then bringing back the allure of gold. And we think that that structural story is not off the table. It's just being crowded out by the near-term rise in real rates.

headline: Mizuho's Varathan sees Fed on prolonged pause but hawkish messaging needed to avoid bond market dislocation
reasoning: Varathan's base case has long anticipated a prolonged fall into late 2025 or early 2026 before the Fed splits into either 2-3 hikes or 2-3 cuts, depending on Middle East outcomes and the resulting inflation-growth trade-offs. The July jobs number was sufficiently soft to argue against rushing into a September hike, keeping a pause as the base case. However, the Fed's credibility was undermined by stumbling during the press conference, weakening confidence in its inflation-fighting resolve. Varathan warns that without unambiguously hawkish messaging around intent, the Fed risks another round of dislocations in the bond market and the dollar.
quote: The base case for us is we had, uh, we had for a long time now, anticipated a prolonged fall into either late this year or early next year, where we saw it splitting into, uh, either a quick succession of 2 to 3 hikes or 2 to 3 cuts, depending on the outcomes in the Middle East and the consequent, um, inflation economy trade offs that, that, that took place. Uh, as of now, I think the jobs number is enough for the, uh, the FOMC to still hang on to a pause. That's to say they don't hike, but my suspicion is that the messaging would have to turn a lot more unambiguously hawkish around intent if they want to avoid, uh, another round of, uh, you know, dislocations in the bond market and all the dollar.
episode_title: The RBA is in its "watch and wait" era

His base case had long anticipated a prolonged pause stretching into late 2024 or early 2025, after which the Fed would move in quick succession with either 2-3 hikes or 2-3 cuts depending on Middle East developments and the consequent inflation-growth trade-off. He also notes the Fed's credibility was somewhat undermined by a stumbling press conference, creating an additional reason to avoid premature tightening.
quote: That's going to be a bit of a demarcation between, uh, the the stumbling, uh, across, you know, the stumbling during the press conference which undermined confidence in the Fed's inflation and carrying, uh, you know, credibility, uh, versus a very soft and, you know, I would say a sufficiently soft job number to say, you know, you shouldn't rush into a hike, uh, in September either. The base case for us is we had, uh, we had for a long time now, anticipated a prolonged fall into either late this year or early next year, where we saw it splitting into, uh, either a quick succession of 2 to 3 hikes or 2 to 3 cuts, depending on the outcomes in the Middle East and the consequent, um, inflation economy trade offs that, that, that took place. Uh, as of now, I think the jobs number is enough for the, uh, the FOMC to still hang on to a pause.
episode_title: The RBA is in its "watch and wait" era

headline: Varathan warns Australian housing market decline will drag on economy via wealth effects and balance sheet risks, complicating RBA's policy path
reasoning: Varathan notes ANZ has forecast a 4.3% decline in capital city housing prices, which will weigh on household balance sheets as servicing costs rise while collateral values fall. This creates a wealth and income effect that softens consumer spending and broader economic activity. The RBA faces a dilemma because housing market deterioration moves counter to ongoing price pressures, forcing a more measured approach. Housing market effects are known to linger for extended periods, making balance sheet risks a key concern for the RBA even as it maintains a hawkish inflation-fighting message.
quote: If you're invested in the housing market, uh, and, you know, servicing mortgages, so on and so forth, uh, that's not going to be a great thing, because if you're looking to, uh, if that declines, you know, asset values for home owners and for mortgage servicing, you know, the, the, the tyrannical, uh, irony here is that your servicing costs go up whereas your collateral value declines. So that's going to leave the economy somewhat softer due to housing and housing related activities... this is where I think the RBI's dilemma and today's justified pause is that's the one policy tool with very far reaching effects. And if the housing market is going one, the, you know, the other way to price pressures, that's where the RBA probably has to, uh, you know, take a far more measured approach because housing market effects can notoriously linger for far longer.
episode_title: The RBA is in its "watch and wait" era

headline: Mizuho's Varathan sees RBA in watch-and-wait mode but retains hawkish optionality, with next move more likely a hike than a cut
reasoning: Varathan argues the RBA has sufficient justification to pause given resilience in the labour market but notes the bank will not discard its readiness to hike. Upside inflation risks from Middle East cost shocks and food price pipeline effects from El Niño keep a hike more probable than a cut as the next move. He acknowledges the binary risk of hike-or-cut could materialise well into 2027. The RBA is also wary of over-tightening financial conditions given the extent of yield rises in USD and GBP, which constrains urgency for further action despite the hawkish signalling remaining in place.
quote: We do see sufficient resilience in the job market, uh, such that more incoming pressures in terms of prices, uh, means that the RBA will keep its vigilance up and definitely keep maximum optionality. So that's to say, whilst they will not sound imminently hawkish, the hawkish views and references and readiness to hike will not be discarded immediately. Uh, and with the rolling, uh, crisis that you just alluded to in the Middle East, which means that any cost shock, uh, the, the or rather, the chances of cost shock remain a fairly significant risk, particularly given that the pipeline effects through food prices exacerbated by the El Nino, are going to come through. Those are sufficient factors to say that the RBA remains ready to hike, so if there was going to be any move. The bet is still for a hike rather than a cut.
episode_title: The RBA is in its "watch and wait" era
